screens.title: The Hardware Description Language (HDL)
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will meet HDL, the compact textual language we use to describe chips. HDL lets you declare a chip's interface and then build it from other chips by listing parts and connecting named pins. You will learn the essential structure — the CHIP declaration, IN and OUT sections, and the PARTS list — and see why HDL models real hardware as a network of components connected by wires. We will walk through how to express single-bit logic, how to declare multi-bit buses and sub-ranges, and how the Hardware Simulator runs test scripts that load, evaluate, and compare outputs automatically. You will also learn common debugging traps, like swapped connections or missing outputs, and why HDL enforces explicit wires instead of nested expressions. By the end you should understand how HDL supports modularity: tested components can be used as black boxes in larger designs. Consider a Mux implemented with And, Or, and Not chips — once tested, it becomes a reliable building block. How will you use this blueprint idea when you design your next chip?

keyIdea.title: HDL = Blueprint for Chips
keyIdea.text: HDL describes a chip as named inputs and outputs plus a PARTS list of component instances wired together, matching physical circuits and enabling modular design.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › The Hardware Description Language
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

HDL: the chip blueprint

Specify a chip's interface, list internal parts, and wire them explicitly. HDL mirrors real hardware connectivity so your designs are testable and modular.

Structure
CHIP ChipName {
  IN a, b, ...;
  OUT out, ...;

  PARTS:
  // internal chip instances
}
Why it matters

HDL forces explicit wires and component instances. That maps directly to physical gates and fosters reliable, testable designs that can be composed into larger systems.

Simulator link

The Hardware Simulator loads HDL, runs test scripts, evaluates outputs, and compares results to expected files for automated verification.

Common pitfall

Forgetting to name an internal wire or swapping connections will make tests fail. HDL does not allow nested expressions; every component must have named outputs.

Explore Key Topics
CHIP Syntax

How to declare IN, OUT and assemble PARTS into a chip definition.

Buses & Sub-busing

Declaring multi-bit inputs and accessing ranges like a[0..15].

Simulator & Tests

Write test scripts that set inputs, eval, output, and compare results automatically.

Visual Concept
CHIP box
Inputs, outputs, internal parts listed inside.
PARTS
Each line instantiates a chip and wires its pins.
Wires
Internal names created implicitly by connecting pins.
Starter Example
CHIP Mux {
  IN a, b, sel;
  OUT out;

  PARTS:
  Not(in=sel, out=notSel);
  And(a=a, b=notSel, out=aAndNotSel);
  And(a=b, b=sel, out=bAndSel);
  Or(a=aAndNotSel, b=bAndSel, out=out);
}

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Our objectives focus on practical mastery of HDL and the simulator. First, you will learn HDL syntax and semantics so you can read and write clear chip specifications. That means knowing the CHIP declaration, the IN and OUT lists, and how PARTS instantiate and wire components. Second, you will be able to write HDL for combinational chips, translating truth tables into instances and explicit internal wires that reflect the signals in hardware. Third, you will use the Hardware Simulator to load HDL files, run test scripts that set inputs and evaluate outputs, and interpret the simulator's discrepancy reports. Finally, you will learn to describe a chips internal parts using other chips as building blocks, treating tested components as black boxes. Each objective trains a concrete skill: writing syntactically correct HDL, generating exhaustive tests, debugging mismatches, and composing modular designs. When you master these four, you can build from gates up to multi-bit structures with confidence. Which objective will you practice first?

screens.title: HDL file structure: CHIP, IN, OUT, PARTS
screens.narratorSegment: An HDL file describes one chip as a declaration with four essential pieces. The CHIP line names the component you are defining. The IN section lists the input pins — the signals the outside world drives. The OUT section lists the output pins that your chip produces. The PARTS section is a list of component instances, each of which is a chip with its own pins. Together, these parts and the named connections between them form the internal wiring of your chip. For example, a Mux declaration names inputs a, b and a selector, and lists Not, And, and Or instances whose outputs are assigned to internal wires. A key point is that internal wires are implicit: naming the same identifier in two different PARTS connections creates a signal net that carries a value. A common misconception is to expect HDL to permit nested expressions or inline gates; HDL models real circuits, so every operation is an instantiated chip with its own output pin. Practically, that means you must give each intermediate signal a name when it is produced by a part. As you read and write HDL, think of the file as a circuit blueprint where PARTS are physical devices and named wires trace their connections. To check your understanding, can you name the inputs, outputs, and the internal wires in a simple Mux declaration?

keyIdea.title: One File, One Chip
keyIdea.text: An HDL file names a single chip and defines its interface and internal composition through explicit part instances and named wires.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › HDL file structure
Definition

CHIP, IN, OUT, PARTS

Each HDL file declares a single chip and maps its internal parts into a network of named wires. This structure mirrors hardware and supports modular composition.

CHIP declaration
Names the chip. Example: CHIP Mux { ... }
IN and OUT
Lists the external pins that form the chip's interface.
PARTS
Instantiates other chips; connections name inputs and outputs to form internal wiring.
Concrete Example
CHIP Mux {
  IN a, b, sel;
  OUT out;

  PARTS:
  Not(in=sel, out=notSel);
  And(a=a, b=notSel, out=aAndNotSel);
  And(a=b, b=sel, out=bAndSel);
  Or(a=aAndNotSel, b=bAndSel, out=out);
}
Key Takeaway

Think of the file as a circuit blueprint: inputs and outputs are ports, PARTS are devices, and matching names create wires between them.

Common Mistake

Expecting nested expressions instead of instantiating parts. HDL requires each operation to be a chip instance with a named output.

screens.title: Pin connections and internal wires
screens.narratorSegment: Pin connections in HDL are written as pinName=value and they form the actual wiring of your chip. The value may be an input pin, an output pin of another part, or a newly named internal wire. Internal wires are created implicitly: when you assign a part's out to a name and then use that same name as an input to another part, HDL treats that name as a signal net connecting the two parts. This is a core idea: HDL models signals as names that carry values between components. Consider the Mux example: Not(in=sel, out=notSel) produces the signal notSel, which is then used by And as an input. A common misunderstanding is to try expressions like And(a=a, b=Not(sel), out=...) — HDL does not support writing Not(sel) inline. Each component must be instantiated so its output gets a name. When debugging, missing wires often appear as unconnected outputs or simulator errors when expected signals are not driven. To reason about connectivity, trace names through PARTS lines and verify that every used name is produced by some part or is a declared input. As practice, write a small PARTS list and mark each name as input, output, or internal wire; this habit prevents swapped connections and naming conflicts.

keyIdea.title: Names = Signals
keyIdea.text: A name used as an output in one PARTS line and an input in another becomes an implicit internal wire that carries a signal between parts.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Pin Connections & Wires
Process Flow

How connections create signals

1. Write PARTS lines where each chip instance lists pinName=value pairs.
2. When a part outputs to a name, that name becomes an internal wire if not declared as an input or output.
3. Reuse that name as a value in another PARTS connection to connect the devices.
4. Verify every used name is either a top-level input/output or produced by some part.
Example trace
Not(in=sel, out=notSel);
And(a=a, b=notSel, out=aAndNotSel);
And(a=b, b=sel, out=bAndSel);
Or(a=aAndNotSel, b=bAndSel, out=out);
Cards
Internal wire
A name assigned as out in one PARTS line and used elsewhere becomes a wire, e.g. notSel.
Declared input
Top-level inputs like sel are sources provided from outside the chip.
Common mistake
Trying to pass an expression instead of naming the output of a part; HDL requires explicit instances.
Key Takeaway

Treat every PARTS out= name as a signal provider and trace it through subsequent PARTS lines to verify connectivity.

screens.title: Mux in HDL — a code walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the Mux example step by step. The Mux has inputs a, b, and sel, and a single output out. The PARTS list instantiates Not, two Ands, and an Or. The Not produces notSel from sel. Then one And computes aAndNotSel using a and notSel, and the other And computes bAndSel using b and sel. Finally the Or combines those two intermediate signals to produce out. Each intermediate name — notSel, aAndNotSel, bAndSel — is an implicit internal wire that connects outputs of some parts to inputs of others. Notice how this structure enforces clarity: every intermediate signal has a name you can inspect in the simulator. An important contrast is functional expressions: you might wish to write out = (sel? b : a) inline, but HDL requires explicit parts. This makes it straightforward to probe any intermediate value while debugging and is faithful to hardware where actual gates drive wires. As you read the code, practice labeling each PARTS line with the source device and the signal it produces. When you simulate, step through inputs and observe how sel governs which And contributes to out. This concrete mapping between code and signal flow is the heart of HDL.

keyIdea.title: Walk the Signals
keyIdea.text: Each PARTS instantiation produces named signals; tracing them in order shows how inputs are combined to form outputs.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Mux Walkthrough
Code
CHIP Mux {
  IN a, b, sel;
  OUT out;

  PARTS:
  Not(in=sel, out=notSel);
  And(a=a, b=notSel, out=aAndNotSel);
  And(a=b, b=sel, out=bAndSel);
  Or(a=aAndNotSel, b=bAndSel, out=out);
}
Annotations
notSel
Produced by Not(in=sel) and used as input to the first And.
aAndNotSel / bAndSel
Intermediate signals that represent the gated contributions of a and b based on sel.
Check

When sel is 0, aAndNotSel should carry a to out; when sel is 1, bAndSel should carry b. The simulator lets you confirm these signals step by step.

screens.title: Declaring buses and And16 example
screens.narratorSegment: HDL supports multi-bit buses by annotating pin names with a width in square brackets, for example a[16] for a 16-bit input. When you declare a bus, you still compose it from 1-bit components: each bit is wired by indexing the bus name with [i]. A canonical example is And16, which computes the bitwise AND of two 16-bit inputs. In HDL you'll write a loop of PARTS lines, one per bit, that instantiate And with a=a[0], b=b[0], out=out[0], and so on up to a[15]. This explicit per-bit wiring makes the internal structure visible and testable. A potential misconception is to think a[16] automatically creates a vector that can be treated as a single signal by 1-bit parts; it doesn't. You must address each bit explicitly or use chips that accept bus ranges. If you later want to build a 16-bit Mux, you can instantiate sixteen 1-bit Mux parts or reuse a prebuilt Mux16 chip when available. Practically, designing with buses teaches you to think about parallel hardware: each bit operates independently, and you confirm correctness by writing test scripts that cover representative patterns like all zeros, all ones, and random mixes. This practice ensures that your bitwise composition matches the expected truth table across every position.

keyIdea.title: Buses are Indexed Groups
keyIdea.text: A multi-bit bus is declared with a width and wired per bit by indexing, so wide chips are built by composing 1-bit parts across indices.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Multi-bit Buses
Definition

Bus declaration and per-bit wiring

Declare inputs like a[16] and instantiate 1-bit parts for each index to implement bitwise operations.

And16 pattern
CHIP And16 {
  IN a[16], b[16];
  OUT out[16];

  PARTS:
  And(a=a[0], b=b[0], out=out[0]);
  ...
  And(a=a[15], b=b[15], out=out[15]);
}
Practical notes
Parallelism
Each bit is independent, so you can reason about correctness per index and run tests with representative patterns.
Reuse
If you have a tested 1-bit component, instantiate it across indices to build a wide component predictably.
Key Takeaway

Buses group bits by name and width; you still wire each bit explicitly when composing from 1-bit parts.

screens.title: Accessing sub-ranges and composing wide Muxes
screens.narratorSegment: Sub-busing lets you pass entire ranges of a bus into a single PARTS instance when that instance accepts a bus of matching width. The syntax uses a[i.. j] to indicate a contiguous subset of bits. For example, Mux4Way16 can be instantiated by passing a[0..15], b[0..15], and a two-bit selector sel[0..1]. This enables concise wiring when a part is designed to operate on a full vector rather than a single bit. Under the hood, the part will expect the listed bus width and internally map its bits to its own PARTS or 1-bit components. A common pitfall is mismatched widths: the range you pass must match the declared width of the sub-chip, otherwise simulation will fail or the intended connections won't be made. Another subtlety: slicing does not create new values by computation; it reuses the existing bits by name. When composing wide Muxes, prefer building and testing a reusable N-bit Mux chip and then passing sub-ranges into it. This keeps your top-level HDL concise and leverages abstraction: once the Mux16 or Mux4Way16 is verified, you can reuse it confidently without reexamining its internals.

keyIdea.title: Ranges Pass Vectors
keyIdea.text: Use a[start..end] to pass contiguous bit ranges into parts; widths must match the expected bus size of the instantiated chip.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Sub-busing & Composition
Hierarchy

Passing sub-ranges into parts

Use a[i..j] to hand a contiguous subset of bits to a part that expects a bus of the same width.

Example call
Mux4Way16(a=a[0..15], b=b[0..15], c=c[0..15], d=d[0..15], sel=sel[0..1], out=out[0..15]);
Notes
Width matching
The sliced range must have the same width the part expects, otherwise connections fail.
Reuse and abstraction
Design and test N-bit components, then pass sub-ranges to use them in larger designs.
Key Takeaway

Sub-busing simplifies wiring when parts accept whole vectors; ensure ranges line up with expected widths.

screens.title: Using the Hardware Simulator
screens.narratorSegment: The Hardware Simulator is your primary feedback tool for HDL development. It follows a simple workflow driven by test scripts. First, the script loads your HDL file. Then it sets specific input values using set commands, runs eval to compute outputs for those inputs, and writes the current outputs with output. The script can also specify an output-file and a compare-to file; compare-to points to a. cmp file containing expected outputs for each test case. When compare-to is present, the simulator compares your outputs to the expected results and reports any discrepancy along with the line where the error occurred. This automated comparison is essential for fast verification. An important practical tip is to write exhaustive test scripts for small chips so every combination is checked. For 3-input chips, that means covering all eight possibilities. A common mistake is to forget to include eval after setting inputs, which leaves outputs stale and causes false failures. Use the simulator's GUI to step through failing cases: it shows the values of internal wires and the outputs of internal parts so you can trace where the behavior deviates from expectation. With consistent testing and careful inspection of mismatched lines, you can quickly isolate connection typos or missing wires.

keyIdea.title: Test-Driven Hardware
keyIdea.text: Write test scripts that load HDL, set inputs, eval, output results, and use compare-to to automate verification and show discrepancies for debugging.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Hardware Simulator
Test Script Steps
1. load ChipName.hdl
2. output-file ChipName.out
3. compare-to ChipName.cmp
4. set inputs, eval, output for each test case
Example commands
set a 0, set b 1, set sel 0, eval, output;
Debugging with the GUI
• When a test fails, the simulator reports the mismatching line and shows values for internal wires.
• Use stepping to observe how each part's outputs evolve across test cases.
• Confirm every internal wire is driven and connected as intended.
Key Takeaway

Automated compare-to is the fastest feedback loop. Always include eval and use exhaustive tests for small chips.

screens.title: Writing test scripts and exhaustive tests
screens.narratorSegment: A robust testing strategy uses exhaustive test scripts for small chips and representative patterns for larger buses. For a 1-bit or 2-bit chip, exhaustive testing means enumerating every input combination in the test script with set, eval, and output commands. The test script should load your HDL, specify an output file, set the inputs for each case, call eval, then output and compare-to the expected file. The compare-to file contains the expected outputs in the same order as your test cases. If compare-to is omitted, you still get output files, but you'll lack automated verification. When writing scripts for buses, include edge cases: all zeros, all ones, alternating bits, and a few random patterns. This combination catches common index wiring mistakes and off-by-one errors in bus slices. A common pitfall is forgetting to include eval between sets and output; eval performs the actual computation, so omitting it yields stale outputs. Another mistake is mismatched output ordering between your script and the. cmp file. Keep the ordering consistent and document which inputs each line represents. Practice by writing a script for a 3-input chip, run it in the simulator, and confirm that compare-to reports zero discrepancies; that builds confidence in your HDL before composing it into larger designs.

narration.text: A robust testing strategy uses exhaustive test scripts for small chips and representative patterns for larger buses. For a 1-bit or 2-bit chip, exhaustive testing means enumerating every input combination in the test script with set, eval, and output commands. The test script should load your HDL, specify an output file, set the inputs for each case, call eval, then output and compare-to the expected file. The compare-to file contains the expected outputs in the same order as your test cases. If compare-to is omitted, you still get output files, but you'll lack automated verification. When writing scripts for buses, include edge cases: all zeros, all ones, alternating bits, and a few random patterns. This combination catches common index wiring mistakes and off-by-one errors in bus slices. A common pitfall is forgetting to include eval between sets and output; eval performs the actual computation, so omitting it yields stale outputs. Another mistake is mismatched output ordering between your script and the. cmp file. Keep the ordering consistent and document which inputs each line represents. Practice by writing a script for a 3-input chip, run it in the simulator, and confirm that compare-to reports zero discrepancies; that builds confidence in your HDL before composing it into larger designs.

keyIdea.title: Exhaustive + Representative Tests
keyIdea.text: Exhaustive scripts for small chips and well-chosen patterns for buses provide the coverage needed to catch wiring and indexing errors before composition.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Test Scripts
Template
load ChipName.hdl,
output-file ChipName.out,
compare-to ChipName.cmp,
output-list a%B3.1.3 b%B3.1.3 sel%B3.1.3 out%B3.1.3;

set a 0, set b 0, set sel 0, eval, output;
set a 0, set b 0, set sel 1, eval, output;
...
Checklist
  • Include eval after set commands so outputs update.
  • Use compare-to for automated verification.
  • Cover all combinations for small chips, edge and random patterns for buses.
  • Keep ordering of outputs consistent with .cmp files.
Key Takeaway

Automation via compare-to is essential; exhaustive tests give confidence for small components before they are reused.

screens.title: Debugging HDL: common mistakes and inspection
screens.narratorSegment: When tests fail, the simulator points you to the case and line where outputs differ. Use that report as your starting point. The simulator's GUI can show the internal state: values of internal wires and outputs of each part. Begin by reproducing the failing test case and then inspect the named intermediate signals that feed the incorrect output. Common mistakes include swapped connections, where a pin is connected to the wrong source; unconnected outputs, where a PARTS instance's out was never used or wrongly named; and using the wrong sub-chip in a PARTS line. Naming conflicts may also occur when two different intended signals share the same identifier accidentally. A practical debugging sequence is: run the failing case, expand the top-level chip in the GUI, locate the part that should produce the suspect signal, and verify its inputs and output. If the output is incorrect, step down into that part or check its PARTS wiring. If outputs are floating or constant, check that each produced name is actually computed by some part or declared input. Keep a checklist next to your test: verify connections, check part types, confirm bus widths, and ensure eval is called between sets and output. This methodical approach turns simulator feedback into precise fixes rather than guesswork.

keyIdea.title: Trace, Inspect, Fix
keyIdea.text: Use simulator discrepancy reports and the GUI's internal wire inspection to trace errors to swapped pins, missing outputs, or wrong component choices.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Debugging HDL
Common Errors
  • Swapped connections (a=sel instead of a=a).
  • Missing or misnamed internal wires.
  • Wrong internal chip used in PARTS.
  • Bus width mismatches when slicing ranges.
Debug Sequence
1. Reproduce the failing test case from the script.
2. Read the simulator's discrepancy line to see which output differs.
3. Inspect internal wires and part outputs in the GUI to trace the incorrect signal.
4. Fix swapped pins, missing outputs, or wrong part names and re-run tests.
Pro tip

Label intermediate names clearly and avoid reusing identifiers, which makes tracing in the simulator much faster.

screens.title: HDL as an abstraction tool
screens.narratorSegment: HDL enforces modularity by making you explicitly instantiate parts and wire them together. This mirrors engineering practice: design a small chip, test it thoroughly, then use it as a black box in larger assemblies. Once a Mux or Adder is verified, other chips can rely on its specified inputs and outputs without knowing how it is implemented. This separation of interface and implementation lets you change internals — perhaps reducing gate count or improving timing — without affecting chips that depend on the interface. A common student misconception is to think HDL forces you to expose internals; in fact, HDL encourages hiding them once tested. In practice, document the interface carefully, include tests that capture expected behavior, and then treat the chip as a component that provides signals described by its OUT pins. When composing many layers, keep tests at each level: unit tests for the small chip and integration tests for the composed chip. This multi-level testing creates confidence that each abstraction boundary is correct. Reflect: when you use a tested chip as a building block, what assumptions do you have about its timing and behavior? Making those assumptions explicit keeps designs robust as complexity grows.

keyIdea.title: Design by Layers
keyIdea.text: Build and verify small chips, then use them as black boxes in higher-level designs to manage complexity and ensure correctness across layers.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Abstraction & Modularity
Principle

Test small, compose large

Verify each chip separately. Then use it as a black box in larger chips without exposing internal details.

Benefits
  • Reduces complexity when designing higher-level chips.
  • Makes debugging localized to the failing component.
  • Allows internal optimization without changing interfaces.
Practice
• Build Not, And, Or and test them.
• Use them to implement Mux and verify the Mux with a test script.
• Treat Mux as a black box when composing larger buses or adders.
Key Takeaway

Abstraction in HDL means verified components become reliable building blocks; test boundaries clearly and reuse with confidence.

screens.title: Practical labs: implement and test basic chips
screens.narratorSegment: Work through small, focused implementations to build confidence. Start with Not implemented from Nand gates and write a complete test script covering both inputs. Next implement And using Nand and Not, then Or using De Morgan's variant built from Nand and Not. For Xor, compose And, Or, and Not to match the truth table; for Mux and DMux, use And, Or, and Not as building blocks. For each chip write a test script that exhaustively sets all input combinations, calls eval, and compares to the provided. cmp file. Use the simulator's discrepancy output to inspect internal wires when a test fails. A practical habit is to make incremental commits: after writing a chip and its test, run the script and fix failures before moving on. This reduces debugging scope and helps you learn the mapping between PARTS lines and signal behavior. When you finish these chips, try composing them into a 16-bit version by instantiating the 1-bit chip across indices and running representative bus tests. This sequence enforces isolation of errors and demonstrates HDL's power: small verified blocks scale predictably into larger designs.

keyIdea.title: Build Incrementally
keyIdea.text: Implement simple chips first and write exhaustive tests; compose verified 1-bit chips into multi-bit versions to scale reliably.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Hands-on Activity
Sequence
  1. Implement Not using only Nand gates; test both inputs.
  2. Implement And using Nand and Not; test exhaustively.
  3. Implement Or via De Morgan using Nand and Not; verify.
  4. Implement Xor from And, Or, Not and test all combos.
  5. Implement Mux and DMux from And/Or/Not; write full tests.
Testing Tips
• Run each chip's test script until it passes before composing.
• Use exhaustive tests for 1-3 input chips to catch all logic faults.
• When composing into buses, test edge cases like all zeros/ones and alternating patterns.
Key Takeaway

Small verified components are the most reliable path to larger, correct chips; practice disciplined test-driven development.

keyIdea.text: Remember file structure, named signals, bus indexing, simulator workflow, and a test-first, modular development approach.

CHIP, IN, OUT, PARTS define the interface and composition of a chip.

In this lesson you will meet HDL, the compact textual language we use to describe chips. HDL lets you declare a chip's interface and then build it from other chips by listing parts and connecting named pins. You will learn the essential structure — the CHIP declaration, IN and OUT sections, and the PARTS list — and see why HDL models real hardware as a network of components connected by wires. We will walk through how to express single-bit logic, how to declare multi-bit buses and sub-ranges, and how the Hardware Simulator runs test scripts that load, evaluate, and compare outputs automatically. You will also learn common debugging traps, like swapped connections or missing outputs, and why HDL enforces explicit wires instead of nested expressions. By the end you should understand how HDL supports modularity: tested components can be used as black boxes in larger designs. Consider a Mux implemented with And, Or, and Not chips — once tested, it becomes a reliable building block. How will you use this blueprint idea when you design your next chip?

Our objectives focus on practical mastery of HDL and the simulator. First, you will learn HDL syntax and semantics so you can read and write clear chip specifications. That means knowing the CHIP declaration, the IN and OUT lists, and how PARTS instantiate and wire components. Second, you will be able to write HDL for combinational chips, translating truth tables into instances and explicit internal wires that reflect the signals in hardware. Third, you will use the Hardware Simulator to load HDL files, run test scripts that set inputs and evaluate outputs, and interpret the simulator's discrepancy reports. Finally, you will learn to describe a chips internal parts using other chips as building blocks, treating tested components as black boxes. Each objective trains a concrete skill: writing syntactically correct HDL, generating exhaustive tests, debugging mismatches, and composing modular designs. When you master these four, you can build from gates up to multi-bit structures with confidence. Which objective will you practice first?

Let's turn the objectives into concrete practice steps you can follow. For understanding HDL syntax, read small HDL files and identify the chip's inputs and outputs, and spot each PARTS instantiation. To practice writing HDL, implement 1-bit chips like Not, And, Or, Xor, and then compose them into Mux and DMux — this forces you to use explicit internal wires. For simulator skills, create test scripts that exhaustively set inputs, run eval, and use compare-to so you get instant feedback. As you build composite chips, document which internal wires are created and why. This practice sequence helps you see modularity: a tested Mux becomes a reliable building block for 16-bit Muxes. A common misconception is that HDL lets you nest expressions; it doesn't. You must instantiate components and name their outputs. Keep testing as you build. Which practice will you schedule first?

An HDL file describes one chip as a declaration with four essential pieces. The CHIP line names the component you are defining. The IN section lists the input pins — the signals the outside world drives. The OUT section lists the output pins that your chip produces. The PARTS section is a list of component instances, each of which is a chip with its own pins. Together, these parts and the named connections between them form the internal wiring of your chip. For example, a Mux declaration names inputs a, b and a selector, and lists Not, And, and Or instances whose outputs are assigned to internal wires. A key point is that internal wires are implicit: naming the same identifier in two different PARTS connections creates a signal net that carries a value. A common misconception is to expect HDL to permit nested expressions or inline gates; HDL models real circuits, so every operation is an instantiated chip with its own output pin. Practically, that means you must give each intermediate signal a name when it is produced by a part. As you read and write HDL, think of the file as a circuit blueprint where PARTS are physical devices and named wires trace their connections. To check your understanding, can you name the inputs, outputs, and the internal wires in a simple Mux declaration?

Pin connections in HDL are written as pinName=value and they form the actual wiring of your chip. The value may be an input pin, an output pin of another part, or a newly named internal wire. Internal wires are created implicitly: when you assign a part's out to a name and then use that same name as an input to another part, HDL treats that name as a signal net connecting the two parts. This is a core idea: HDL models signals as names that carry values between components. Consider the Mux example: Not(in=sel, out=notSel) produces the signal notSel, which is then used by And as an input. A common misunderstanding is to try expressions like And(a=a, b=Not(sel), out=...) — HDL does not support writing Not(sel) inline. Each component must be instantiated so its output gets a name. When debugging, missing wires often appear as unconnected outputs or simulator errors when expected signals are not driven. To reason about connectivity, trace names through PARTS lines and verify that every used name is produced by some part or is a declared input. As practice, write a small PARTS list and mark each name as input, output, or internal wire; this habit prevents swapped connections and naming conflicts.

Let's walk through the Mux example step by step. The Mux has inputs a, b, and sel, and a single output out. The PARTS list instantiates Not, two Ands, and an Or. The Not produces notSel from sel. Then one And computes aAndNotSel using a and notSel, and the other And computes bAndSel using b and sel. Finally the Or combines those two intermediate signals to produce out. Each intermediate name — notSel, aAndNotSel, bAndSel — is an implicit internal wire that connects outputs of some parts to inputs of others. Notice how this structure enforces clarity: every intermediate signal has a name you can inspect in the simulator. An important contrast is functional expressions: you might wish to write out = (sel? b : a) inline, but HDL requires explicit parts. This makes it straightforward to probe any intermediate value while debugging and is faithful to hardware where actual gates drive wires. As you read the code, practice labeling each PARTS line with the source device and the signal it produces. When you simulate, step through inputs and observe how sel governs which And contributes to out. This concrete mapping between code and signal flow is the heart of HDL.

HDL supports multi-bit buses by annotating pin names with a width in square brackets, for example a[16] for a 16-bit input. When you declare a bus, you still compose it from 1-bit components: each bit is wired by indexing the bus name with [i]. A canonical example is And16, which computes the bitwise AND of two 16-bit inputs. In HDL you'll write a loop of PARTS lines, one per bit, that instantiate And with a=a[0], b=b[0], out=out[0], and so on up to a[15]. This explicit per-bit wiring makes the internal structure visible and testable. A potential misconception is to think a[16] automatically creates a vector that can be treated as a single signal by 1-bit parts; it doesn't. You must address each bit explicitly or use chips that accept bus ranges. If you later want to build a 16-bit Mux, you can instantiate sixteen 1-bit Mux parts or reuse a prebuilt Mux16 chip when available. Practically, designing with buses teaches you to think about parallel hardware: each bit operates independently, and you confirm correctness by writing test scripts that cover representative patterns like all zeros, all ones, and random mixes. This practice ensures that your bitwise composition matches the expected truth table across every position.

Sub-busing lets you pass entire ranges of a bus into a single PARTS instance when that instance accepts a bus of matching width. The syntax uses a[i.. j] to indicate a contiguous subset of bits. For example, Mux4Way16 can be instantiated by passing a[0..15], b[0..15], and a two-bit selector sel[0..1]. This enables concise wiring when a part is designed to operate on a full vector rather than a single bit. Another subtlety: slicing does not create new values by computation; it reuses the existing bits by name. When composing wide Muxes, prefer building and testing a reusable N-bit Mux chip and then passing sub-ranges into it. This keeps your top-level HDL concise and leverages abstraction: once the Mux16 or Mux4Way16 is verified, you can reuse it confidently without reexamining its internals.
